title: Microsoft Fabric Architecture Strategy — Operating Model to Migration Sequencing
purpose: Shows the architecture decisions a Fabric platform team actually makes: the tenant/domain/workspace containment hierarchy, workloads landing on one shared OneLake, the governance and capacity boundaries that attach to that shared layer, the deployment-pipeline promotion path, and the private-link network-isolation trade-off teams hit during migration.
accessibleSummary: A tenancy-hierarchy diagram at the top shows a Microsoft Entra tenant containing domains, domains containing workspaces, and workspaces both drawing compute from a capacity and holding items created by role-oriented workloads (Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Power BI) that all persist to OneLake. Below that, four architecture-decision panels branch off the shared OneLake layer: a governance panel showing Purview's tenant-to-domain-to-workspace policy hierarchy; a capacity panel showing the recommended multi-capacity isolation pattern by environment and workload tier; a deployment-pipeline panel showing Dev-to-Test-to-Production promotion gated by pull requests; and a network-isolation panel comparing tenant-wide private links against workspace-level private links, with a warning about the all-or-nothing tenant-wide trade-off. A SaaS framing note at the bottom states there is no separate infrastructure layer to provision underneath any of this.
longDescription: This diagram grounds the Architecture Strategy topic: the operating model, platform boundaries, governance, capacity, and architecture decisions a team must make deploying Microsoft Fabric. The top zone establishes the containment hierarchy that every other decision nests inside — one Fabric tenant maps one-to-one to one Microsoft Entra tenant; domains group workspaces into business-aligned units (recommended at roughly 15-20 workspaces per domain to limit sprawl) so administrators can delegate governance below the tenant level; workspaces hold items created by role-oriented workloads and draw their compute from an assigned capacity. Every workload's data lands on the same OneLake layer regardless of which engine wrote it. From that shared foundation, four architecture-decision panels branch off: governance operates as a three-tier hierarchy (tenant defaults, domain overrides, workspace controls) covering data-estate management, protection, discovery, and monitoring; capacity is the isolation and chargeback boundary, and the documented pattern is splitting capacities by environment stage plus reserving separate capacity for contention-sensitive executive reporting; Deployment Pipelines promote items Dev-to-Test-to-Production with pull-request gates and Variable Libraries injecting per-environment connection strings; and network isolation via private links is a real architectural fork — tenant-wide private links are all-or-nothing and break on-premises gateways and several Power BI features, while workspace-level private links (F-SKU only) allow a mixed public/private deployment. A closing note reinforces that none of this sits on a separate infrastructure layer to provision — Fabric is SaaS, so these are configuration and governance decisions, not resource-provisioning decisions.

nodes.label: Tenant → domain → workspace hierarchy
nodes.summary: One Fabric tenant maps one-to-one to one Microsoft Entra tenant; domains group workspaces for delegated governance, and workspaces hold items and draw compute from a capacity.
nodes.detail: A Fabric tenant is a single organizational instance of the service aligned one-to-one with a Microsoft Entra tenant. Inside it, workspaces act as collaboration containers that hold items, draw compute from a capacity, and control who can access their contents. Domains sit between tenant and workspace: they let an organization group workspaces into logical business areas (for example Finance or Marketing), giving administrators a level above the workspace at which to delegate management and apply governance policies. Domain architecture is recommended to align to functional business units rather than mirror org-chart structure, with a practical guideline of roughly 15-20 workspaces per domain to limit sprawl.
nodes.whyItMatters: This containment chain is the first architecture decision every other node on this diagram nests inside — governance delegation, capacity assignment, and workload placement are all scoped by where a workspace sits in the tenant/domain hierarchy, so getting the domain boundary wrong (e.g. mirroring the org chart instead of business capability) propagates governance sprawl downstream.

evidence.note: A Fabric tenant is a single organizational instance aligned one-to-one with a Microsoft Entra tenant; workspaces act as collaboration containers holding items, drawing compute from a capacity, and controlling access.
Domains group workspaces into logical business areas, giving administrators a delegation level above the workspace for management and governance policy.
Domain architecture is recommended to align to functional business units rather than org-chart structure, with a practical guideline of roughly 15-20 workspaces per domain to limit sprawl.

processing: Establish the one Fabric tenant bound to the organization's Entra tenant
Group workspaces into domains aligned to functional business units, not the org chart
Create workspaces underneath each domain scoped to a team or bounded data product
Assign each workspace to a capacity for compute and to a domain for delegated governance
outputs: A domain-scoped set of workspaces with delegated admin authority
A stable place for capacity assignment and governance policy to attach
drill.example: A retail organization creates a 'Merchandising' domain containing 14 workspaces (one per regional team plus shared platform workspaces), delegating domain-level governance to a merchandising data lead instead of routing every policy change through tenant admins.
controls: Domain boundary definition (business capability vs org chart)
Workspace count per domain (target 15-20 before splitting)
Which settings are delegated to domain admins vs kept tenant-wide
failureModes: Domains mirroring the org chart instead of business capability, so a reorg forces a governance re-architecture
Workspace sprawl inside a single domain past the ~15-20 guideline, making delegated administration unmanageable

nodes.label: Role-oriented workloads over one OneLake
nodes.summary: Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Power BI, and other role-oriented workloads all create items inside a workspace, and every workload persists its data to the same tenant-wide OneLake.
nodes.detail: Fabric organizes its functionality into role-oriented workloads — Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence, and more — each of which lets a workspace create its own item types (pipelines, lakehouses, warehouses, semantic models). Beneath every workload sits a shared platform layer used consistently by every experience: OneLake for storage, Copilot for embedded AI, and Purview for governance. Because Fabric is SaaS, users never deal with Azure infrastructure concepts such as resource groups, RBAC, Azure Resource Manager, or redundancy configuration — there is no separate infrastructure layer to provision underneath any workload.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the decision that makes workload choice reversible: because every workload's output lands on the same OneLake regardless of engine, an architecture team can add or swap workloads inside a workspace without a data-migration project, and governance/capacity controls attach once at the platform layer instead of once per workload.

evidence.note: Fabric organizes functionality into role-oriented workloads (Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Data Warehouse, Databases, Real-Time Intelligence). Beneath the workloads sits a shared platform layer of OneLake, Copilot, and Purview used by every experience.
Because Fabric is SaaS, users never deal with Azure infrastructure concepts such as resource groups, RBAC, Azure Resource Manager, or redundancy configuration.

inputs: A workspace scoped to a domain and assigned a capacity
The data shape and consumption pattern the domain needs to serve
processing: Enable the role-oriented workload(s) that fit the domain's ingestion, transform, and consumption needs inside the workspace
Each workload creates its own item types (pipelines, lakehouses, warehouses, semantic models)
Every item's tabular data persists automatically to the same tenant-wide OneLake as open Delta Parquet
outputs: Items owned by the workspace, addressable by every other Fabric engine through OneLake
No workload-private storage silo to reconcile later
drill.example: A finance workspace enables Data Factory to orchestrate nightly ingestion, Data Warehouse for the T-SQL-first ledger transformation, and Power BI for the reporting layer — three workloads, one workspace, one OneLake copy of the underlying Delta tables.
controls: Which workloads are enabled per workspace
Item-level ownership and naming inside the workspace
failureModes: Standing up a workload-private data store instead of writing to OneLake, breaking the one-copy guarantee for that dataset
Assuming Fabric SaaS abstracts away governance and capacity decisions the same way it abstracts away infrastructure provisioning

nodes.label: OneLake: the shared storage layer
nodes.summary: OneLake is the tenant-wide logical data lake every workload writes to and reads from — the platform-layer service the whole hierarchy above is built to feed.
nodes.detail: Beneath every role-oriented workload sits a shared platform layer used consistently by every Fabric experience: OneLake for storage, Copilot for embedded AI, and Purview for governance. OneLake holds the tabular data every workload item creates as open Delta Parquet, addressable by every compute engine (Spark, T-SQL, Analysis Services) without a per-engine copy.
nodes.whyItMatters: OneLake is the architectural pivot the rest of this diagram hangs off: because it is one shared layer rather than per-workload storage, governance and capacity controls documented in the panels below can attach once at the platform boundary instead of being re-implemented per workload.

evidence.note: Beneath the workloads sits a shared platform layer of three services used consistently by every experience: OneLake for storage, Copilot for embedded AI, and Purview for governance.

inputs: Delta Parquet tables written by any enabled workload in any workspace across the tenant
processing: Hold each workload's tabular output as open Delta Parquet under the tenant's single OneLake namespace
Expose that same physical data to every other Fabric engine without a copy step
Serve as the attachment point for the governance and capacity controls shown in the panels below
outputs: One physical, addressable copy of each dataset for every engine and every governance/capacity control to reference
drill.example: A Data Warehouse item and a Data Engineering lakehouse in different workspaces both persist to the same tenant OneLake; a Power BI semantic model reads either directly without an import step.
controls: Whether an item's data is native OneLake or a shortcut to external storage
failureModes: Writing data outside OneLake from a workload, losing the one-copy guarantee for that dataset and forcing governance/capacity controls to be reapplied elsewhere

nodes.label: Governance: tenant → domain → workspace policy
nodes.summary: Purview-backed governance operates as a three-tier hierarchy — tenant-wide defaults, domain-level overrides, and workspace-level controls — covering data-estate management, protection, discovery, and monitoring.
nodes.detail: Fabric organizes its governance surface into four functional areas: managing the data estate (admin portal, domains, workspaces, capacities, metadata scanning), securing and protecting data (sensitivity labels, DLP, auditing), encouraging discovery and trust (OneLake catalog, endorsement, tags, lineage), and monitoring activity (monitoring hub, capacity metrics, admin monitoring workspace). Governance settings operate in a three-tier hierarchy: tenant-wide defaults set by Fabric admins, domain-level overrides applied by domain admins for delegated settings, and workspace-level controls managed by workspace owners for the most granular scope.
nodes.whyItMatters: The three-tier hierarchy is the architectural mechanism that makes domain delegation from the tenancy panel actually enforceable — a domain admin can tighten a tenant default for their business area without filing a request to tenant admins, which is what keeps governance from becoming a central bottleneck as the tenant scales.

evidence.note: Fabric's governance surface covers four functional areas: managing the data estate, securing/protecting data, discovery and trust, and monitoring activity.
Governance settings operate in a three-tier hierarchy: tenant-wide defaults, domain-level overrides applied by domain admins, and workspace-level controls managed by workspace owners.

inputs: Tenant-wide governance defaults set by Fabric admins
processing: Fabric admins set tenant-wide defaults for the four governance areas
Domain admins override delegated settings for their business area
Workspace owners apply the most granular, workspace-level controls
Sensitivity labels, DLP, and lineage tracking apply through the OneLake catalog regardless of which tier set the policy
outputs: A governance policy resolved per item from the most specific applicable tier
An audit and lineage trail visible in the OneLake catalog
drill.example: A tenant admin sets a default sensitivity-label policy tenant-wide; the Finance domain admin overrides it to require a stricter 'Confidential' default for their domain's workspaces; a workspace owner inside that domain still cannot loosen the domain override.
controls: Which settings tenant admins choose to leave delegable to domains
Workspace-level access controls within domain constraints
failureModes: Domain admins unaware a setting is not delegable, assuming a workspace-level fix is possible when it isn't
Governance policy drift when tenant defaults change but domain overrides are never revisited

nodes.label: Capacity: environment & workload isolation
nodes.summary: Capacities are the compute isolation and chargeback boundary; the documented pattern splits capacities by environment stage and reserves separate capacity for contention-sensitive workloads.
nodes.detail: Each Fabric capacity is a distinct resource pool living inside a Microsoft Entra tenant; the SKU size determines how much compute power it provides. Capacities serve as isolation boundaries for compute resources and chargebacks, and the recommended practice is to split capacities by environment stage (development, test, acceptance, production) to achieve workload isolation and cost attribution. A documented multi-capacity architecture pattern adds a larger production capacity for mission-critical workloads, a small development/test capacity for authoring, and optionally a separate capacity reserved for high-priority executive-facing reports that need isolation from other contention.
nodes.whyItMatters: Capacity assignment is where the tenancy hierarchy's workspace boundary becomes an operational guarantee: because Fabric throttles per capacity rather than per tenant, splitting capacities by environment and contention-sensitivity is what keeps one team's dev workload from starving another team's production reports.

evidence.note: Each Fabric capacity is a distinct resource pool living inside a Microsoft Entra tenant; the SKU size determines how much compute power the capacity provides.

Capacities serve as isolation boundaries for compute resources and chargebacks; the recommended practice is splitting capacities by environment stage (dev/test/acceptance/production) for workload isolation and cost attribution.

A documented multi-capacity architecture pattern: a larger production capacity for mission-critical workloads, a small development/test capacity for authoring and testing, and optionally a separate capacity reserved for high-priority executive-facing reports needing isolation from other contention.

inputs: Contention sensitivity of specific high-priority workloads
processing: Assign each workspace's environment-stage workspaces to a dedicated capacity rather than sharing one capacity across stages
Size the production capacity for mission-critical workload demand
Optionally split off a dedicated capacity for executive-facing reports that cannot tolerate contention from other workloads
outputs: Cost attribution per environment/business area via capacity-level billing
Throttling isolation, since Fabric enforces throttling per capacity, not tenant-wide
drill.example: A tenant runs a Production F64 capacity for the merchandising domain's live reports, a shared Dev/Test F8 capacity for all domains' pre-production workspaces, and a dedicated F16 capacity reserved solely for the CFO's executive dashboard so a dev workload spike can never throttle it.
controls: Capacity SKU size per environment stage
Whether a contention-sensitive workload gets its own dedicated capacity
failureModes: Sharing one capacity across dev, test, and production so a runaway dev job throttles production reporting
No dedicated capacity for executive-facing content, so unrelated workload spikes visibly degrade leadership-facing dashboards

nodes.label: Deployment Pipelines: Dev → Test → Production
nodes.summary: Items are promoted across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces through Deployment Pipelines, with Variable Libraries injecting per-environment connection strings and pull-request gates before production promotion.
nodes.detail: The documented deployment pattern uses Deployment Pipelines to promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, with Variable Libraries injecting environment-specific connection strings and pull-request gates required before promotion to production.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the CI/CD mechanism that operationalizes the environment-stage capacity split above: without a controlled promotion path, splitting capacities by environment only isolates compute, not the actual release process that moves an item from authoring to production.

evidence.note: Recommended deployment pattern: Deployment Pipelines promote items across Dev, Test, and Production workspaces, with Variable Libraries injecting environment-specific connection strings and pull-request gates required before promotion to production.

inputs: Items authored and validated in a Dev workspace
Environment-specific configuration values held in a Variable Library
processing: Promote items from Dev to Test via Deployment Pipelines
Variable Libraries swap in Test-scoped connection strings and configuration at promotion time
Require an approved pull request before the Test-to-Production promotion step executes
Variable Libraries swap in Production-scoped configuration on final promotion
outputs: A validated, environment-appropriate item deployed to Production without manual config edits
An auditable promotion history per pipeline stage
drill.example: A pipeline item authored in Dev references a Dev-scoped SQL connection string via a Variable Library; promoting through Test then Production automatically swaps in the Test and Production connection strings respectively, with the Production promotion blocked until a reviewer approves the pull request.
controls: Which items are included in the deployment pipeline's content scope
Variable Library value sets per stage
Whether pull-request review is enforced as a hard gate
failureModes: Hardcoding a connection string instead of using a Variable Library, so promotion silently points production at a dev/test resource
Skipping the pull-request gate under deadline pressure, losing the review step meant to catch breaking changes before production

nodes.label: Network isolation: tenant-wide vs workspace-level private link
nodes.summary: Tenant-wide private links are all-or-nothing and break on-premises gateways; workspace-level private links (F-SKU only) allow a mixed public/private deployment instead.
nodes.detail: Fabric offers two distinct private link scopes: a tenant-level option covering the entire tenant at any paid SKU, generally available since May 2024, and a workspace-level option restricted to individual workspaces on F SKUs only, generally available since October 2025. The tenant-level model is all-or-nothing; the workspace-level model permits a mixed public-private deployment. On-premises data gateways cannot register and will not function when tenant-level Block Public Internet Access is enabled, with no supported workaround. Private links are a viable architectural choice only for pure cloud-to-cloud workloads on F SKUs that have no dependency on on-premises data gateways; for organizations lacking an explicit regulatory mandate for network-level isolation, Conditional Access combined with an IP firewall is a documented lighter-weight alternative.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a real fork in the architecture, not a tuning knob: choosing tenant-wide private link scope commits the whole tenant to losing on-premises gateway connectivity and several Power BI features, so architecture teams migrating a hybrid estate need the workspace-level option or an alternative like Conditional Access plus IP firewall instead of defaulting to the broader tenant-wide toggle.

evidence.note: Fabric offers two private link scopes: tenant-level (all-or-nothing, any paid SKU, GA since May 2024) and workspace-level (F SKUs only, GA since October 2025, permits mixed public-private deployment).
On-premises data gateways cannot register and will not function when tenant-level Block Public Internet Access is enabled; there is no supported workaround.

Private links are viable only for pure cloud-to-cloud F-SKU workloads with no on-premises gateway dependency; Conditional Access plus an IP firewall is a documented lighter-weight alternative absent a regulatory mandate.

inputs: Whether the estate has any on-premises data gateway dependency
Regulatory requirement (or absence of one) for network-level isolation
processing: Confirm no on-premises gateway dependency exists before considering any private link scope
If isolation is required tenant-wide and the estate is pure cloud-to-cloud, evaluate tenant-level private links on any paid SKU
If only specific workspaces need isolation, evaluate workspace-level private links, available on F SKUs only, to keep the rest of the tenant public
If no explicit regulatory mandate exists, evaluate Conditional Access plus an IP firewall as a lighter-weight alternative to either private link scope
outputs: A chosen network-isolation posture that either preserves or knowingly breaks on-premises gateway and specific Power BI feature availability
drill.example: A hybrid organization migrating from an on-premises warehouse still depends on an on-premises gateway for a legacy source feed; the architecture team rejects tenant-wide private link, since it would deregister that gateway with no workaround, and instead isolates only the F64 workspace handling the regulated dataset with workspace-level private link.
controls: Private link scope selection (tenant vs workspace vs none)
SKU tier (workspace-level private link requires F SKU)
Whether Conditional Access plus IP firewall substitutes for private link entirely
failureModes: Enabling tenant-wide Block Public Internet Access without auditing on-premises gateway dependencies first, silently breaking legacy connectivity tenant-wide
Provisioning a new capacity while tenant-level private links are active without accounting for the documented DNS propagation delay of up to 24 hours

nodes.label: SaaS: no separate infrastructure layer
nodes.summary: Because Fabric is a single SaaS control plane, none of the decisions above involve provisioning Azure resource groups, ARM templates, or redundancy settings underneath.
nodes.detail: Microsoft Fabric is architected as a single SaaS control plane where compute engines share one capacity (F-SKU) and billing surface. Because Fabric is SaaS, users never deal with Azure infrastructure concepts such as resource groups, RBAC, Azure Resource Manager, or redundancy configuration.
nodes.whyItMatters: This framing note closes the diagram deliberately: every architecture decision documented above (domains, workspaces, capacity, governance, deployment pipelines, network isolation) is a configuration and policy decision inside one SaaS control plane, not an infrastructure-provisioning decision — architects coming from IaaS/PaaS backgrounds should not look for a resource-group or VNet layer that does not exist in Fabric's model.

evidence.note: Microsoft Fabric is architected as a single SaaS control plane where compute engines share one capacity (F-SKU) and billing surface; users never deal with Azure infrastructure concepts such as resource groups, RBAC, ARM, or redundancy configuration.

inputs: All architecture decisions made across the tenancy, workload, governance, capacity, deployment, and network-isolation panels above
processing: Confirm no Azure resource group, ARM template, or VNet needs to be provisioned to realize any decision above
Treat capacity SKU sizing, not infrastructure sizing, as the resource-planning axis
outputs: An architecture expressed entirely in Fabric-native constructs: tenant, domain, workspace, capacity, item
drill.example: A team migrating from a self-managed Synapse/Azure SQL estate initially plans an Azure landing zone for Fabric before realizing capacity provisioning replaces the resource-group/VNet exercise entirely.
controls: None — this is a platform characteristic, not a configurable control
failureModes: Architecture teams importing IaaS/PaaS habits (separate infra sizing, resource-group planning) that don't map onto Fabric's SaaS model, wasting planning effort on a layer that doesn't exist

network isolation is a governance/security decision

walkthrough.title: 1. Start with the containment hierarchy
walkthrough.explanation: Every architecture decision nests inside the tenant → domain → workspace hierarchy: one Fabric tenant per Entra tenant, domains grouping workspaces by business capability (not org chart), each workspace holding items and drawing compute from an assigned capacity.

walkthrough.title: 2. Workloads create items inside a workspace
walkthrough.explanation: Role-oriented workloads — Data Factory, Data Warehouse, Power BI, and others — create their own item types inside a workspace. Choosing a workload is choosing an execution engine, not a separate storage silo.

walkthrough.title: 3. Everything lands on the same OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: Whichever workload is chosen, its tabular data persists to the same tenant-wide OneLake as open Delta Parquet. This shared layer is what lets governance and capacity controls attach once instead of per workload.

walkthrough.title: 4. Governance resolves through three tiers
walkthrough.explanation: Tenant-wide defaults, domain-level overrides, and workspace-level controls resolve governance policy per item, covering data-estate management, protection, discovery, and monitoring.

walkthrough.title: 5. Capacity isolates compute by environment
walkthrough.explanation: The documented pattern splits capacities by environment stage — dev/test/acceptance/production — plus an optional dedicated capacity for contention-sensitive executive reporting, since Fabric throttles per capacity, not tenant-wide.

walkthrough.title: 6. Promote items through Deployment Pipelines
walkthrough.explanation: Deployment Pipelines move items Dev to Test to Production, with Variable Libraries swapping environment-specific connection strings and a pull-request gate required before production promotion.

walkthrough.title: 7. Decide the network-isolation scope deliberately
walkthrough.explanation: Tenant-wide private links are all-or-nothing and break on-premises gateways with no workaround; workspace-level private links (F SKU only) or Conditional Access plus an IP firewall are the alternatives for a hybrid or mixed estate.

walkthrough.title: 8. Remember: no infrastructure layer underneath
walkthrough.explanation: Every decision above is configuration and policy inside one SaaS control plane — there is no Azure resource group, ARM template, or VNet layer to separately provision.
